title: How Much Should You Have Saved by 30? The Honest Version
description: How much should you have saved by 30? What the popular benchmarks assume, why they miss real lives, and what a late start can still do.
figureLabel: salary is a rule of thumb

cover.alt: A cake with a lit number 30 candle next to a pink piggy bank

keywords: how much should i have saved by 30 savings by age 30 retirement savings by age benchmark fidelity
takeaways: The "one year of salary by 30" benchmark assumes you saved 15% from age 25.
If you are behind, the gap is smaller than it looks, and a steady monthly amount still does a lot.
Get any employer match first, then pick an amount your budget can survive in a bad month.
body:
Search "how much saved by 30" and you will get the same answer on almost every page: one year of your salary. If you are nowhere near that number, most of those articles then do one of two things. They talk to you as if you have been careless, or they quietly assume you started a full-time job at 22 and have been saving ever since. Plenty of people did neither. Maybe you started work at 26. Maybe you earn a low wage, work part-time, or are still paying off student debt. Maybe you do not even live in the US, which is where that famous number comes from.

This is the honest version. It explains where the benchmark comes from, why so many people miss it, and the part most articles skip: the actual catch-up math, worked out in full, for people starting late or starting small. There is no shame in any of this. The numbers are kinder than you probably expect.

## The benchmark everyone quotes

The figure comes from Fidelity, one of the largest retirement plan providers in the US. Fidelity's guideline is to aim for at least 1x your salary saved by age 30, then 3x by 40, 6x by 50, 8x by 60, and 10x by 67. It is the most repeated set of milestones in personal finance, which is why it shows up everywhere.

Notice what the target is a multiple of: your salary, not a fixed dollar amount. The scary headline version, "you should have $60,000 by 30," comes from applying the rule to a typical full-time wage. Experian, using Bureau of Labor Statistics figures, puts median annual earnings for 25- to 34-year-olds in the US at $59,280 for the first quarter of 2026, which rounds to that $60,000 target. But if you earn $32,000 a year, your by-30 target under this same guideline is $32,000. If you work part-time and earn $21,000, the target is $21,000. The rule scales down with your life, even if the headlines do not.

## The fine print nobody reads

Fidelity is open about the assumptions underneath its milestones, and they matter. The numbers are built around a person who saves 15% of their income every year starting at age 25, including any employer match, keeps more than half of that money in stocks, retires at 67, and wants to carry on living at roughly the same standard in retirement.

Read that again and compare it with a real life. Saving 15% from age 25 assumes you had a job at 25 that paid enough to save from. It assumes no years lost to study, caring for family, illness, or patchy work. It assumes rent left something over. If you started at 27, or your wage is too low for 15% to be realistic, or your twenties went to clearing debt, you are not behind on the plan. You were never on that version of the plan in the first place. Fidelity itself describes the milestones as aspirational goalposts, not a pass or fail line.

Two more things worth knowing. First, the 1x figure refers to retirement savings. Your emergency fund and money saved for nearer goals sit outside it, so do not compare your total bank balance against it. Second, Fidelity is not the only voice. T. Rowe Price, another large investment firm, suggests a gentler ladder: half your salary by 30 and 1.5x by 35.

## Where people your age actually stand

So what do real 30-year-olds have? According to Fidelity figures reported by Experian, the average 401(k) balance for 30- to 34-year-olds was $45,700 in the fourth quarter of 2024. And an average is pulled upward by a minority of very large balances, so the typical person has less than that. The Federal Reserve's 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances found that people under 35 had average retirement savings of $49,130, again an average, again lifted by high earners at the top.

In other words, missing the 1x mark at 30 is the normal outcome, not a personal failure. The reasons are ordinary. Starting wages are low. Rent in most cities takes a far bigger share of a first salary than it used to. Student loan payments compete with saving for the same dollars each month. Many people simply start later, because their first stable job arrives at 26 or 28 rather than 22. Part-time and gig workers often have no workplace pension at all, so nothing is saved unless they set it up themselves. None of that is a character flaw. It is just the starting position, and starting positions can be worked with.

## The catch-up math nobody shows you

Here is the part the benchmark articles leave out. What does starting late actually cost, and what can a modest monthly amount still do? The table below is an illustration, not a prediction. It assumes money saved every month grows at 6% a year, every year, which real markets never do in a straight line. The amounts and ages are made up so you can see the shape of the maths.

| If you start at | Saving per month | Worth by age 40 | Worth by age 60 | You paid in by 60 |
|-----------------|------------------|-----------------|-----------------|-------------------|
| 24              | $150            | about $48,200  | about $228,700 | $64,800          |
| 24              | $300            | about $96,300  | about $457,500 | $129,600         |
| 27              | $150            | about $35,300  | about $186,200 | $59,400          |
| 27              | $300            | about $70,600  | about $372,400 | $118,800         |
| 30              | $150            | about $24,600  | about $150,700 | $54,000          |
| 30              | $300            | about $49,200  | about $301,400 | $108,000         |

Three things stand out. First, look at the last two columns. Someone who starts at 30 and saves $300 a month pays in $108,000 by age 60, yet the pot holds about $301,400. Growth did the rest of the work, even with a late start. Starting late costs you something, but it does not cost you anything like everything.

Second, the honest price of waiting. Saving $300 a month from 24 instead of 30 produces about $156,000 more by 60, even though the early starter only pays in $21,600 more. Those six years matter. But read it the other way as well: the person who starts at 30 still ends up with a serious sum, roughly two-thirds of the early starter's pot. Late is a disadvantage. It is not a disaster.

Third, small amounts are not pointless. Even $150 a month from age 30 builds to about $150,700 by 60 in this illustration, on $54,000 of payments. If $150 is out of reach, $75 still beats zero by a wide margin over 30 years.

One more worked example, because it is the situation many readers are actually in. Say you turn 30 with nothing saved and start putting away $250 a month. At the same assumed 6% growth, you would have about $41,000 by 40 and about $251,000 by 60, having paid in $90,000. To hit the full $60,000 benchmark by 40 from a standing start at 30, you would need roughly $366 a month at that growth rate. To reach half of it, $30,000, you would need roughly $183 a month. Pick the version you can keep going with, because a plan you keep beats a bigger plan you quit by spring.

## A sensible order if you are starting from zero

If the benchmark feels a long way off, work on the order of things rather than the size of things.

Start with a small cash buffer, even $500 to $1,000, in an easy-access account. It stops one bad week from landing on a credit card and undoing your progress. Read next: [How to Build an Emergency Fund on a Low Income](/blog/emergency-fund-on-a-small-income/).

Next, if your employer offers a pension or 401(k) match, contribute enough to get the full match before anything else. That match is part of how Fidelity's model reaches its 15%, and it is the closest thing to free money most of us will ever be offered.

Then deal with expensive debt. Credit card interest usually runs far ahead of anything your savings will earn, so clearing it often does more for your future balance than investing early would. Read next: [How to Pay Off Credit Card Debt Fast](/blog/pay-off-credit-card-debt-fast/).

After that, set a monthly amount you can genuinely afford and raise it slowly, a little at a time, ideally whenever your pay goes up. A budget built around your real income makes this far easier to stick to. Read next: [How to Make a Budget When You Earn Less Than $1,000 a Month](/blog/budget-on-less-than-1000-a-month/). And when you are ready to put long-term money into investments rather than a savings account, small monthly amounts are a perfectly reasonable way in. Read next: [How to Start Investing With Little Money](/blog/start-investing-with-little-money/). If you are in the US and weighing up account types, this comparison helps. Read next: [Roth IRA vs 401(k) for Beginners](/blog/roth-ira-vs-401k-beginners/).

## What if you are not in the US?

The 1x figure is American, built around US salaries, US retirement accounts, and Social Security covering part of retirement income. If you are in the UK, Canada, or Australia, the machinery around you is different. The UK has the State Pension and workplace pensions with employer contributions. Canada has the Canada Pension Plan alongside RRSPs and TFSAs. In Australia, employers pay superannuation contributions on top of wages for most workers, so a pot may be building for you already even if you have never saved a cent yourself.

The multiple-of-salary idea still works as a rough yardstick anywhere, though. Having something close to one year of your own pay set aside for the long term by around 30 puts you in decent shape in any of these countries. What changes is where the money should live and how much the state adds later. Run the table above in your own currency. Growth does not care which symbol sits in front of the number.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is $10,000 saved by 30 a bad result?

No. On a low income, $10,000 is real money, and it usually means you have built the saving habit, which is the hard part. The benchmark is a multiple of salary, so on a $25,000 income you are already 40% of the way to the Fidelity version of the target, and close to the gentler T. Rowe Price one.

### Does my emergency fund count toward the 1x target?

Not in Fidelity's version. The 1x figure is about retirement savings. Your emergency fund still counts toward your overall security, and for most people starting out it should come first. Just keep the two buckets separate in your head so you do not feel behind twice for the same money.

### Should I invest or pay off student debt first?

Look at the interest rate. Debt charging well above what investments could reasonably earn, especially credit card debt, usually comes first. With lower-rate student loans, many people split the difference: pay the loan, get any employer match, and invest a small amount alongside.

### I am 32 and have saved nothing. Is it too late?

No. The table above starts at 30, and starting at 32 with the same monthly amounts lands you in a similar place, a little lower. You have around three decades before a typical retirement age. That is a long time for regular saving to work, and it is far more than many people who retire comfortably ever had.

### How much should I save each month in my 30s if I am behind?

Work backwards from an amount you can keep up every month, not from the benchmark. In the illustration above, $183 a month from 30 builds about $30,000 by 40 at 6% growth, and $250 a month builds about $41,000. Choose a figure your budget survives in a bad month, then raise it when your pay rises.

### Does the money have to be in a retirement account?

The guideline is about money set aside for the long term, and retirement accounts usually give tax advantages that help it grow. Where exactly it belongs depends on your country and your plans. Money you might need within a few years, such as a house deposit, normally belongs somewhere safer and easier to reach, not in the same pot.

## The honest answer

How much should you have saved by 30? If you followed a textbook path, about one year of your salary. If your path involved a late start, a low wage, debt, or a life that did not run to plan, then the honest target is simpler: something saved, growing, and added to every month. The gap between starting at 24 and starting at 30 is real, but it is measured in a slightly smaller pot at 60, not in success and failure. Pick a monthly amount, start it this month, and let the maths in the table do its slow work.

Disclaimer: This article is general information for education only. It is not financial, tax, or investment advice, and the growth figures in the table and examples are illustrations based on an assumed 6% annual return. Real investment returns vary and can be negative. For advice about your own situation, speak to a qualified, regulated adviser in your country.
